doc.title: Onaje Allan Gumbs interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 12, 2001

title: Future projects and the eclectic approach
summary: He discusses a Blue Note recording, The Art of Accompaniment, acting, film scoring and continuing eclecticism.

story.theme_name: Still working: current gigs, upcoming projects and plans
story.community_name: What's next: upcoming tours, records and plans

blocks.x: Listen, what’s in the near future for you, we’re going to have to wrap up here.

I have two projects. I did a “Live at the Blue Note” which I’m very proud of. And I finally did a Henry Mancini tune, I talked about earlier on. I had never done Henry Mancini in my book. So I did “Dreamsville” from Peter Gunn. And did more piano. Because I was always behind the scenes, getting the saxophone player up there, the trumpet player, but now I’m doing the front line. I have a studio project I did on my own with some great people on it, that I’m trying to bring out independently. I’m working on a concert with the great singer Carmen Lundy to fashion a thing called “The Art of Accompaniment.” Okay? That hopefully we’ll take around to a lot of different schools, © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -18-

high schools, colleges, to talk about the relationship between the pianist and the vocalist, on all different kinds of levels. And the preparation needed from both. I’ve done some acting. I acted in a play, a professional production of a play called “Lady Day at Emerson’s Bar & Grill,” and I play Lady Day’s pianist, Jimmy Powers. I had a few lines, but it was still a whole new kind of experience. So that’s something I may even check out a little more. And I’d like to do some more scoring. I did a film for Danny Glover in ’94 for Showtime, so that experience was something that has opened me up also. But the eclectic approach that I learned from being very young is something I’m going to continue, not just as a solid jazz pianist, although I hate the word “jazz.” I hate the word “jazz” because so many things go with it that have connotations, okay? But in lieu of a better term to come down the pike, as a solid jazz musician. But also to be involved in other sincere expressions, which may take me to Latin, Brazilian, hip hop, R&B. To me if you are a serious musician about what you’re trying to do, I don’t care what you’re playing. Because we can communicate. Because we’re doing something that a whole lot of people were doing, accounting and Internet can’t do, and that’s really play notes, bring these notes together, and move people without words. Everybody can’t do that or else everybody would be a musician. You see? So that’s what I want to do. And finally to get my name to be something that people will say — well who was that? Or when’s he coming out with something? No, I’ve got something new out, I’ve got something current out, I’m who I am and I want to finally, for 2001 set the record straight, and not to be confused with Najee.
